value.overview: The White-throated Flycatcher (Empidonax albigularis) is a small tyrant flycatcher of Mexico and Central America. It is named for its conspicuous white throat, which contrasts with its brownish upperparts, pale yellowish underparts, and buff wing bars. The species usually occupies open or semi-open habitats rather than dense forest. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon and locally distributed bird, with records from highland valleys, foothills, wetlands, grasslands, and other brushy areas.
value.classification: The White-throated Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Empidonax. It is closely related to other small, visually similar Empidonax flycatchers, which are often difficult to identify without careful attention to plumage, habitat, and voice.
value.identification: This is a small, compact flycatcher with a brownish head and back, two pale buff wing bars, a whitish eye-ring, and yellowish to pale olive underparts. Its strongest field mark is the bright white throat, sharply contrasting with the darker upper breast. The bill is broad at the base, with a dark upper mandible and paler lower mandible. Identification can be difficult because several Empidonax species share similar shapes and wing markings; the call is often useful.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Mexico south through Central America to Panama. In Costa Rica it is locally distributed, especially from about 500 to 1,500 meters along the western and southern slopes of Irazú and the Caribbean-facing slopes of the Guanacaste, Tilarán, and Central Volcanic ranges. It also occurs in intermontane valleys of the southern Pacific lowlands, with lower-elevation records from wetlands and grasslands. Typical habitat includes wet meadows, marsh edges, brushy fields, hedgerows, riparian thickets, clearings, and second-growth vegetation.
value.migrationStatus: The White-throated Flycatcher is resident or seasonally elevational in Costa Rica rather than a regular long-distance migrant. Birds occur in the country's highlands year-round in some areas, while others may move to lower elevations outside the breeding season. Costa Rican lowland records are scattered and may include local elevational movements or migrants from farther north; the timing and extent of these movements are not fully understood.
value.breeding: Breeding information is better documented in northern Central America than in Costa Rica, but the species is considered a breeding resident in parts of the Costa Rican highlands. It generally nests in open or semi-open areas near water, including riparian scrub, wet clearings, marsh margins, and young second growth. The nest is an open cup made from grasses and other plant fibers, usually placed low in a shrub or small tree. Breeding activity elsewhere in Central America is concentrated mainly from April through July or August.
value.dietFeeding: The White-throated Flycatcher feeds mainly on insects and other small arthropods. It typically hunts from a low exposed perch, making short sallies to catch flying insects and sometimes returning to the same perch. It may also glean prey from leaves and stems. In Costa Rica, suitable feeding sites include marsh edges, grassy clearings, brushy pasture, hedgerows, and open woodland margins. Small fruits may occasionally supplement its primarily insect-based diet.
value.behavior: This flycatcher is usually encountered singly or in pairs and often remains inconspicuous in dense grass or low shrubbery. It perches quietly before making short, quick flights after insects. When returning to a perch, it may flick or quiver its wings and tail, a useful behavioral clue. Males defend breeding territories with repeated calls. The species tends to favor edges and semi-open vegetation, where scattered perches provide clear views over nearby ground and vegetation.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered stable or not known to be declining at a rate that approaches a threatened category. Detailed population estimates are limited, especially for local populations in Costa Rica.
